A '''ballistic missile submarine''' is a [[submarine]] capable of deploying [[submarine-launched ballistic missile]]s (SLBMs) with [[nuclear warhead]]s. These submarines became a major weapon system in the [[Cold War]] because of their [[deterrence theory|nuclear deterrence]] capability. They can fire missiles thousands of kilometres (miles) from their targets, and [[acoustic quieting]] makes them difficult to detect (see [[acoustic signature]]), thus making them a survivable deterrent in the event of a [[Pre-emptive nuclear strike|first strike]] and a key element of the [[mutual assured destruction]] policy of nuclear deterrence. Many ballistic missile submarine policies also include provisions for nuclear [[First strike (nuclear strategy)|first strike]] as well. For these reasons, 70% of nuclear warheads in the [[United States]] are carried by ballistic missile submarines.<ref name="apps.dtic.mil">{{Cite web | author=Rafal, A. S. | year=2021 | title=THE FUTURE OF SUBMARINE WARFARE: NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES ARE THE BEDROCK OF NAVAL WARFARE, OR MAYBE NOT. | publisher=Joint Forces Staff College-NDU, Joint Advanced Warfighting School | url=https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/trecms/pdf/AD1153995.pdf}}</ref>

The deployment of ballistic missile submarines is dominated by the [[Columbia-class submarine|United States]],  [[Russia]] (following the collapse of the [[Soviet Union]]) and [[China]]. Smaller numbers are in service with [[France]], the [[United Kingdom]] and [[India]].

[[North Korea and weapons of mass destruction|North Korea]] is also suspected to have an experimental submarine that is diesel-electric powered.<ref name="James Kraska, Raul A. Pedrozo 2022 139">{{cite book|title=Disruptive Technology and the Law of Naval Warfare|author=James Kraska, Raul A. Pedrozo|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|year=2022|page=139}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite news|title=North Korea fires likely submarine-launched ballistic missile, South Korea says|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/nkorea-fires-unidentified-projectile-off-its-east-coast-skorea-military-2022-05-07/|publisher=[[Reuters]]|date=2022-05-07}}</ref> [[Israel and nuclear weapons|Israel]] also has diesel-electric submarines carrying nuclear weapons, however their nuclear warheads are mounted onto [[cruise missile]]s, not onto [[ballistic missile]]s.

Ballistic missile submarines should be distinguished from so-called [[nuclear submarine]]s, which does not refer to a submarine carrying nuclear weapons, but instead refers to submarines with a [[Nuclear marine propulsion|nuclear propulsion engine]].

== History ==
The first sea-based missile deterrent forces were a small number of conventionally powered [[cruise missile submarine]]s and surface ships fielded by the United States and the Soviet Union in the 1950s, deploying the [[Regulus missile|Regulus I missile]] and the Soviet [[SS-N-3 Shaddock|P-5 Pyatyorka]] (also known by its [[NATO reporting name]] SS-N-3 Shaddock), both land attack [[cruise missile]]s that could be [[submarine-launched cruise missile|launched from surfaced submarines]]. Although these forces served until 1964 and (on the Soviet side) were augmented by the nuclear-powered [[Echo-class submarine|Project 659]] (Echo I class) cruise-missile submarines, they were rapidly eclipsed by SLBMs carried by nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines beginning in 1960.{{sfn|Gardiner|Chumbley|1995|pp=352–353, 549, 553–554}}

===Ballistic missile submarine origins===
[[File:I400 2.jpg|thumb|The {{sclass|I-400|submarine|1}}s are considered the strategic predecessors to today's ballistic submarines.]]
The [[Imperial Japanese Navy]] {{sclass|I-400|submarine|1}}s are considered the strategic predecessors to today's ballistic submarines, especially to the Regulus missile program, which began about a decade after World War II.<ref>{{citation |first=Phil |last=Zimmer |title=Japan's Underwater Aircraft Carriers |url=http://warfarehistorynetwork.com/daily/wwii/japans-underwater-aircraft-carriers/ |work=warfarehistorynetwork.com |date=2017-01-05 |access-date=2 March 2018 |archive-date=4 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190904073116/http://warfarehistorynetwork.com/daily/wwii/japans-underwater-aircraft-carriers }}</ref>

During World War II, German researchers developed the [[V-2 rocket|A4]] (V2), the first ballistic missile. Toward the end of the war, a V2 version was developed at the [[Peenemünde Army Research Center|Peenemünde Army Research Station]] to be towed in a launch container behind a submarine. Each submarine was to tow up to three of these {{convert|36|m|adj=on}} containers, manned by ten soldiers, through the [[North Sea]]. Off [[England]], the container would have been brought to the surface and the missiles fired. Prototypes were already being tested on the [[Baltic Sea|Baltic coast]] before the project had to be abandoned in 1945 with the evacuation of [[Peenemünde]]. Three containers were already under construction at that time. The commander of the Army Experimental Station, [[Walter Dornberger]], described the project as "not unpromising".<ref>Polmar, 2003, S. 103 f.</ref>

The first nation to field ballistic missile submarines was the Soviet Union, whose first experimental vessel was a converted [[Zulu-class submarine|Project 611]] (Zulu IV class) diesel-powered submarine equipped with a single ballistic missile launch tube in its sail. This submarine launched the world's first SLBM, an [[R-11FM]] (SS-N-1 Scud-A, naval modification of SS-1 [[Scud]]) on 16 September 1955.<ref name="Wade R-11">{{cite web |url=http://www.astronautix.com/lvs/r11.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020309175348/http://www.astronautix.com/lvs/r11.htm |archive-date=March 9, 2002 |title=R-11 |access-date=23 April 2011 |last=Wade |first=Mark |publisher=[[Encyclopedia Astronautica]]}}</ref>

Five additional Project V611 and AV611 (Zulu V class) boats became the world's first operational ballistic submarines with two R-11FM missiles each, entering service in 1956–57.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://russianships.info/eng/submarines/project_611.htm|title=Large submarines – Project 611|access-date=26 July 2015}}</ref> They were followed by a series of 23 specifically designed [[Golf-class submarine|Project 629]] (Golf class) boats, completed 1958–1962, with three vertical launch tubes incorporated in the sail/fin of each submarine.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://russianships.info/eng/submarines/project_629.htm|title=Ballistic missile submarines – Project 629|access-date=26 July 2015}}</ref> The initial [[R-13 (missile)|R-13]] (SS-N-4) ballistic missiles could only be launched with the submarine on the surface and the missile raised to the top of the launch tube, but were followed by [[R-21 (missile)|R-21]] (SS-N-5) missiles beginning in 1963, which were launched with the submarine submerged.

The world's first operational nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine was {{USS|George Washington|SSBN-598}} with 16 [[Polaris missile|Polaris A-1]] missiles, which entered service in December 1959 and conducted the first SSBN deterrent patrol November 1960 – January 1961.<ref>{{YouTube|pDruXY-jvA8|"Man and the FBM: The US Navy deploys its 1st Polaris Ballistic Missile Subs"}}</ref> (The [[United States Navy]]'s [[Hull classification symbol#Submarine type|hull classification symbols]] for nuclear ballistic missile submarines are '''SSBN''' – the ''SS'' denotes submarine, the ''B'' denotes [[ballistic missile]], and the ''N'' denotes that the submarine is [[Nuclear submarine|nuclear powered]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://doni.daps.dla.mil/Directives/05000%20General%20Management%20Security%20and%20Safety%20Services/05-00%20General%20Admin%20and%20Management%20Support/5030.8B.pdf |title=SECNAVINST 5030.8 |publisher=United States Navy |date=21 November 2006 |access-date=10 September 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140722222518/http://doni.daps.dla.mil/Directives/05000%20General%20Management%20Security%20and%20Safety%20Services/05-00%20General%20Admin%20and%20Management%20Support/5030.8B.pdf |archive-date=22 July 2014 |df=dmy-all }}</ref>) The Polaris missile and the first US SSBNs were developed by a Special Project office under Rear Admiral [[William Raborn|W. F. "Red" Raborn]], appointed by [[Chief of Naval Operations]] Admiral [[Arleigh Burke]]. ''George Washington'' was redesigned and rebuilt early in construction from a {{sclass|Skipjack|submarine|0}} fast attack submarine, USS ''Scorpion'', with a {{convert|130|ft|m|abbr=on}} missile compartment welded into the middle. Nuclear power was a crucial advance, allowing a ballistic missile submarine to remain undetected at sea by remaining submerged or occasionally at [[periscope]] depth ({{convert|50|to|55|ft|m|abbr=on}}) for an entire patrol.

A significant difference between US and Soviet SLBMs was the fuel type; all US SLBMs have been solid fueled while all Soviet SLBMs before 1980 were liquid fueled. The USSR and subsequently Russia deployed three different SLBM types with solid fuel ([[R-31 (missile)|R-31]] in 1980, [[R-39 Rif]] in 1983, and [[RSM-56 Bulava]] in 2018). However, these did not replace liquid-fueled SLBMs in service, and new liquid-fueled SLBMs were developed and introduced ([[R-29RM Shtil|R-29RM]] introduced in 1986, [[R-29RMU Sineva|R-29RMU]] introduced in 2007) after deployment of the R-31 and R-39.

With more missiles on one US SSBN than on five Golf-class boats, the Soviets rapidly fell behind in sea-based deterrent capability. The Soviets were only a year behind the US with their first nuclear powered ballistic missile boat, the [[Soviet submarine K-19|ill-fated ''K-19'']] of [[Hotel-class submarine|Project 658]] (Hotel class), commissioned in November 1960. However, this class carried the same three-missile armament as the Golfs. The first Soviet nuclear submarine with 16 missiles was the [[Yankee-class submarine|Project 667A]] (Yankee class), the first of which entered service in 1967, by which time the US had already commissioned 41 SSBNs, nicknamed the "[[41 for Freedom]]".{{sfn|Gardiner|Chumbley|1995|p=403}}<ref>{{cite web |url = http://russianships.info/eng/submarines/project_667a.htm |title = Nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines – Project 667A |access-date=26 July 2015 }}</ref>

The United Kingdom's first nuclear ballistic missile submarine was the {{sclass|Resolution|submarine|0}} of four submarines built for the [[Royal Navy]] as part of the [[UK Polaris programme]]. The first to be completed was {{HMS|Resolution|S22|2}}, laid down in February 1964 and launched in September 1966. After commissioning in 1967, a period of sea trials followed, culminating in the test firing of a Polaris missile from the [[Eastern Range|USAF Eastern Test Range]] off [[Cape Kennedy]] in February 1968. ''Resolution'' commenced her first operational patrol in June 1968.

France's first nuclear ballistic submarine followed very closely. The first French SLBM submarine, [[French submarine Redoutable (S611)|Le ''Redoutable'']] was laid down in 1964 in [[Constructions Mécaniques de Normandie|Cherbourg]] and launched in March 1967. ''Le Redoutable'' entered operational service in December 1971 and was the first of a series of six ships, with a 7,500-ton displacement and equipped with 16 French-made [[M1 (missile)|M1]] missiles.

=== Deployment and further development ===
The short range of the early SLBMs dictated basing and deployment locations. By the late 1960s the [[UGM-27 Polaris|UGM-27 Polaris A-3]] missile was deployed on all US and UK ballistic missile submarines. Its range of {{convert|4600|km|nmi}} was a great improvement on the {{convert|1900|km|nmi|adj=on}} range of Polaris A-1.  The A-3 also had three warheads that landed in a pattern around a single target.{{sfn|Friedman|1994|pp=199–200}}{{sfn|Polmar|1981|pp=131–133}} The Yankee class was initially equipped with the [[R-27 Zyb]] (SS-N-6) missile with a range of {{convert|2400|km|nmi}}.

The US was much more fortunate in its basing arrangements than the Soviets. Thanks to [[NATO]] and the US possession of [[Guam]], US SSBNs were permanently forward deployed at Advanced Refit Sites in [[Holy Loch]], [[Scotland]] and [[Naval Station Rota|Rota, Spain]] for [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] and [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] areas, and Guam for the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]] areas, by the middle 1960s resulting in short transit times to patrol areas near the Soviet Union. With two rotating crews per SSBN, about one-third of the total US force could be in a patrol area at any time. The Soviet bases, in [[Severomorsk]] near [[Murmansk]] for the Atlantic and the [[Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky]] area for the Pacific, required their submarines to make a long transit through NATO-monitored waters in the Atlantic to their mid-ocean patrol areas to hold the [[Continental United States]] (CONUS) at risk.

US SSBN submarine missions usually last for approximately ninety days (the maximum duration is limited by the supply of food and other consumables that can be carried on board, as well as crew endurance, rather than by the amount of the nuclear fuel on board) and occurs with 18 months maintenance and repair breaks.<ref name="apps.dtic.mil"/> Such a relatively short mission duration resulted in only a small percentage of the Soviet force occupying patrol areas at any time and was a great motivation for longer-range Soviet SLBMs, which would allow them to patrol close to their bases in areas sometimes referred to as "deep bastions". The missiles were the [[R-29 Vysota]] series (SS-N-8, SS-N-18, SS-N-23), equipped on [[Delta-class submarine|Projects 667B, 667BD, 667BDR, and 667BDRM]] (Delta I through Delta IV classes).{{sfn|Gardiner|Chumbley|1995|pp=355–357}} The SS-N-8, with a range of {{convert|7700|km|nmi}}, entered service on the first Delta-I boat in 1972, before the Yankee class was even completed. A total of 43 Delta-class boats of all types entered service 1972–1990, with the SS-N-18 on the Delta III class and the [[R-29RM Shtil]] (SS-N-23) on the Delta IV class.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://russianships.info/eng/submarines/project_667b.htm |title = Nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines – Project 667B |access-date=26 July 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://russianships.info/eng/submarines/project_667bd.htm |title=Nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines – Project 667BD |access-date=26 July 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://russianships.info/eng/submarines/project_667bdr.htm |title = Nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines – Project 667BDR |access-date=26 July 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://russianships.info/eng/submarines/project_667bdrm.htm |title = Nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines – Project 667BDRM |access-date=26 July 2015}}</ref> The new missiles had increased range and eventually Multiple Independently Targeted Re-entry Vehicles ([[MIRV]]), multiple warheads that could each hit a different target.{{sfn|Gardiner|Chumbley|1995|pp=355–357}}

The Delta I class had 12 missiles each; the others have 16 missiles each. All Deltas have a tall superstructure (aka casing) to accommodate their large liquid-fueled missiles.

=== Poseidon and Trident I ===
Although the US did not commission any new SSBNs from 1967 through 1981, they did introduce two new SLBMs. Thirty-one of the 41 original US SSBNs were built with larger diameter launch tubes with future missiles in mind. In the early 1970s the [[Poseidon missile|Poseidon (C-3) missile]] entered service, and those 31 SSBNs were backfitted with it.<ref>Friedman, p. 201</ref> Poseidon offered a massive MIRV capability of up to 14 warheads per missile. Like the Soviets, the US also desired a longer-range missile that would allow SSBNs to be based in [[Contiguous United States|CONUS]]. In the late 1970s the [[UGM-96 Trident I|Trident I (C-4) missile]] was backfitted to 12 of the Poseidon-equipped submarines.{{sfn|Gardiner|Chumbley|1995|p=553}}{{sfn|Friedman|1994|p=206}} The SSBN facilities of the base at Rota, Spain were disestablished and the [[Naval Submarine Base King's Bay]] in [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] was built for the Trident I-equipped force.

=== Trident and Typhoon submarines ===
[[File:US Navy 101029-N-1325N-005 The Ohio-class ballistic submarine USS Alabama (SSBN 731) returns to Naval Base Kitsap from a deterrent patrol.jpg|right|upright=1.35|thumb|{{USS|Alabama|SSBN-731|6}}, an {{sclass|Ohio|submarine|0}} (aka Trident) submarine]]

Both the United States and the Soviet Union commissioned larger submarines designed for new missiles in 1981. The American large SSBN was the {{sclass|Ohio|submarine|4}}, also called the "Trident submarine", with the largest SSBN armament ever of 24 missiles, initially Trident I but built with much larger tubes for the [[UGM-133 Trident II|Trident II (D-5) missile]], which entered service in 1990.{{sfn|Friedman|1994|pp=206–207}}{{sfn|Gardiner|Chumbley|1995|p=554}} The entire class was converted to use Trident II by the early 2000s. When the {{USS|Ohio|SSBN-726|6}} commenced sea trials in 1980, two US {{sclass|Benjamin Franklin|submarine|0}} SSBNs had their missiles removed to comply with [[SALT]] treaty requirements; the remaining eight were converted to [[attack submarines]] (SSN) by the end of 1982. These were all in the Pacific, and the Guam SSBN base was disestablished; the first several ''Ohio''-class boats used new Trident facilities at [[Naval Submarine Base Bangor]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]]. Eighteen ''Ohio''-class boats were commissioned by 1997,{{sfn|Gardiner|Chumbley|1995|p=613}} four of which were converted to [[cruise missile submarine]]s (SSGN) in the 2000s to comply with [[START I]] treaty requirements.

[[File:Typhoon3.jpg|right|thumb|A [[Typhoon-class submarine|Project 941]] (Typhoon-class) nuclear ballistic missile submarine]]
The Soviet large nuclear ballistic missile submarine was the [[Typhoon-class submarine|Project 941 ''Akula'']], more famously known as the Typhoon class (and not to be confused with the [[Akula-class submarine|Project 971 ''Shchuka'']] attack submarine, called "Akula" by NATO). The Typhoons were the largest submarines ever built, at 48,000 tons submerged (more than 2½ times the displacement of the ''Ohio''-class). They were armed with 20 of the new [[R-39 Rif]] (SS-N-20) missiles. Six Typhoons were commissioned 1981–1989.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://russianships.info/eng/submarines/project_941.htm |title = Nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines – Project 941 |access-date=26 July 2015 }}</ref>

The United Kingdom commissioned the 15,600-ton {{sclass|Vanguard|submarine|2}} in 1993, to carry up to 16 Trident II missiles. France commissioned in 1997 the 12,600-ton {{sclass|Triomphant|submarine|2}}, equipped with up to 16 French-made [[M45 (missile)|M45]] missiles.

===Post-Cold War===
With the [[collapse of the Soviet Union]] and the end of the [[Cold War]] in 1991, construction of new nuclear submarines by Russia was put on hold for over ten years and was slowed in the United States. Additionally the US rapidly decommissioned its 31 older remaining SSBNs, with a few converted to other roles, and the base at Holy Loch in Scotland was disestablished. Most of the former Soviet nuclear submarine force was gradually scrapped under the provisions of the [[Nunn–Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction]] agreement through 2012.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dtra.mil/Missions/Verifying.aspx |title=Verifying |access-date=26 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905130451/http://www.dtra.mil/Missions/Verifying.aspx |archive-date=5 September 2015 }}</ref>

The Russian ballistic missile submarine force then stood at six Delta IVs, three Delta IIIs, and a lone Typhoon used as a testbed for new missiles (the R-39s unique to the Typhoons were reportedly scrapped in 2012). Upgraded missiles such as the [[R-29RMU Sineva]] (SS-N-23 Sineva) were developed for the Deltas. In 2013 the Russians commissioned the first {{sclass|Borei|submarine|1}}, also called the ''Dolgorukiy'' class after the lead vessel. By 2015 two others had entered service. This class is intended to replace the aging Deltas, and carries 16 solid-fuel [[RSM-56 Bulava]] missiles, with a reported range of {{convert|10000|km|nmi}} and six MIRV warheads. The US {{sclass|Columbia|submarine|1}} is set to replace the ''Ohio''-class, with construction beginning in 2020.

The United Kingdom and France are set to replace in the early 2030s their current fleets composed respectively of  [[Vanguard-class submarine|''Vanguard'']] and [[Triomphant-class submarine|''Triomphant'']] with third generation 
[[Dreadnought-class submarine|''Dreadnought'']] and unnamed 
[[SNLE 3G]] SLBMs.

In 2009, [[India]] launched the first of its indigenously built {{sclass|Arihant|submarine|1}}s.<ref>{{cite news |url = http://blogs.reuters.com/india/2009/07/31/indias-nuclear-submarine-dream-still-miles-to-go/|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090801160631/http://blogs.reuters.com/india/2009/07/31/indias-nuclear-submarine-dream-still-miles-to-go/|archive-date = 1 August 2009|work=[[Reuters]] |title=India's nuclear submarine dream, still miles to go|date=31 July 2009|access-date=24 January 2011}}</ref> The submarines are armed with [[Sagarika (missile)|K15]] and [[K-4 (missile)|K-4 ]]ballistic missiles. Follow on variants with longer range ballistic missiles called [[K-5 (ballistic missile)|K-5]] and [[K-6 (missile)|K6]] are in works.

North Korea test-fired ballistic missiles from submarines in 2021<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/nkorea-says-it-conducted-successful-missile-test-submarine-kcna-2021-10-19/|title=N.Korea confirms submarine launch of new ballistic missile}}</ref> and 2022.<ref name=":0" />

==Purpose==
{{further|Second strike|Nuclear triad|Attack submarine|Cruise missile submarine}}

Ballistic missile submarines differ in purpose from attack submarines and cruise missile submarines. Attack submarines specialize in combat with other vessels (including enemy submarines and merchant shipping), and cruise missile submarines are designed to attack large warships and tactical targets on land. However, the primary mission of the ballistic missile boat is [[deterrence theory|nuclear deterrence]]. They serve as the third leg of the [[nuclear triad]] in countries that also operate nuclear-armed land based missiles and aircraft. Accordingly, the mission profile of a ballistic missile submarine concentrates on remaining undetected, rather than aggressively pursuing other vessels.<ref name=":1" />

Ballistic missile submarines are designed for [[stealth technology|stealth]] to avoid detection at all costs, and that makes nuclear power, allowing almost the entire patrol to be conducted submerged, very important. They also use many sound-reducing design features, such as [[anechoic tile]]s on their hull surfaces, carefully designed propulsion systems, and machinery mounted on vibration-damping mounts. The invisibility and mobility of nuclear ballistic missile submarines offer a reliable means of deterrence against an attack (by maintaining the threat of a [[second strike]]), as well as a potential surprise [[Pre-emptive nuclear strike|first strike]] capability.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Ballistic Missile Submarines |website=Commander, Submarine Force, U.S. Pacific Fleet |url=https://www.csp.navy.mil/SUBPAC-Commands/Submarines/Ballistic-Missile-Submarines/ |access-date=2024-05-23}}</ref>

== Armament ==
{{Main|Submarine-launched ballistic missile}}

[[File:USS Sam Rayburn (SSBN-635) missile hatches.jpg|thumb|upright|{{USS|Sam Rayburn|SSBN-635|6}} showing the hatches for the [[UGM-27 Polaris]] missiles]]

In most cases, nuclear ballistic missile submarines generally resemble attack subs of the same generation, with extra length to accommodate SLBMs, such as the Russian [[R-29 (missile)|R-29]] (SS-N-23) or the [[NATO]]-fielded and American-manufactured [[UGM-27 Polaris|Polaris]], [[UGM-73 Poseidon|Poseidon]], and [[Trident missile|Trident-II]] missiles. Some early models had to surface to launch their missiles, but modern vessels typically launch while submerged at [[keel depth]]s of usually less than {{convert|50|m|ft}}. Missiles are launched upwards with an initial velocity sufficient for them to pop above the surface, at which point their rocket motors fire, beginning the characteristic parabolic climb-from-launch of a ballistic missile. Compressed air ejection, later replaced by gas-steam ejection, was developed by Captain Harry Jackson of Rear Admiral [[William Raborn|Raborn's]] Special Project Office when a proposed missile elevator proved too complex.{{sfn|Friedman|1994|p=194}} Jackson also derived the armament of 16 missiles used in many SSBNs for the {{sclass|George Washington|submarine|4}} in 1957, based on a compromise between firepower and hull integrity.{{sfn|Friedman|1994|pp=195–196}}

==Terminology and locations==
=== United States and United Kingdom ===
In the US Navy, SSBNs are sometimes called Fleet Ballistic Missile submarines, or FBMs. In [[wikt:Appendix:U.S. Navy slang#B|US naval slang]], ballistic missile submarines are called ''boomers''. In the UK, they are known as ''bombers''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.royalnavy.mod.uk/The-Fleet/Submarines/Ballistic-Submarines|title=Submarine Service – Royal Navy|access-date=26 July 2015}}</ref> In both cases, SSBN submarines operate on a two-crew concept, with two complete crews – including two captains – called ''Gold'' and ''Blue'' in the United States, ''Starboard'' and ''Port'' in the United Kingdom. The designation ''SSBN'' is also used throughout NATO under STANAG 1166.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fas.org/irp/doddir/other/nato2008a.pdf|title=NATO glossary of abbreviations used in NATO documents and publications (AAP-11) |website=Federation of American Scientists |publisher=[[NATO]]|access-date=1 February 2014}}</ref>

=== France ===
The [[French Navy]] commissioned its first ballistic missile submarines as ''SNLE'', for ''Sous-marin Nucléaire Lanceur d'Engins'' (lit. "nuclear-powered device-launching submarines"). The term applies both to ballistic missile submarines in general (for instance "British SNLE" occurs<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.netmarine.net/bat/smarins/triompha/index.htm |title=SNLE-NG ''Le Triomphant'' |publisher=netmarine.net |access-date=19 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140521212804/http://www.netmarine.net/bat/smarins/triompha/index.htm |archive-date=May 21, 2014 }}</ref>) and, more technically, as a specific classification of the {{sclass|Redoutable|submarine (1967)|4}}. Its successor, the {{sclass|Triomphant|submarine|4}}, is referred to as SNLE-NG (''Nouvelle Génération'', "New Generation"). The two crews used to maximise the availability time of the boats are called {{lang|fr|bleu}} (blue) and {{lang|fr|rouge}} (red) crews.

=== Soviet Union and Russian Federation ===
The Soviets called this type of ship ''RPKSN''<ref>''РПКСН'' ''Ракетный подводный крейсер стратегического назначения'' (Raketny Podvodnyy Kreiser Strategicheskogo Naznacheniya)</ref> (lit. "Strategic Purpose Underwater Missile Cruiser"). This designation was applied to the {{sclass2|Typhoon|submarine|4}}. Another designation used was ''PLARB''(''«ПЛАРБ»'' – подводная лодка атомная с баллистическими ракетами, which translates as "Nuclear Submarine with Ballistic Missiles"). This designation was applied to smaller submarines such as the Delta class. After a peak in 1984 (following [[Able Archer 83]]), Russian PLARB deterrence patrols have declined to the point where there is less than one patrol per sub each year and at best one sub on patrol at any time. Hence the Russians did not use multiple crews per boat.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blogs.fas.org/security/2013/05/russianssbns/ |title=Russian SSBN Fleet: Modernizing But Not Sailing Much |website=Federation of American Scientists |date=3 May 2013 |access-date=19 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131217214149/http://blogs.fas.org/security/2013/05/russianssbns/ |archive-date=December 17, 2013 }}</ref> However, the situation changed ca. 2008, when, first time in years, Russia had 10 submarine missile cruisers on patrol.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kristensen |first=Hans |date=2009-02-17 |title=Russian Strategic Submarine Patrols Rebound |url=https://fas.org/publication/russia/}}</ref> One of these submarines was ''Ryazan'', that travelled fully submerged under an icesheet from [[Severomorsk]] base on the [[Barentz Sea]] to [[Vladivostok]] on the [[Sea of Japan]] in just one month.<ref>{{Cite web |title=K-44 Ryazan |url=http://rusnavy.com/nowadays/strength/submarines/ryazan/ |website=RussNavy.com}}</ref>

[[Category:Ballistic missile submarines| ]]
extract:
A ballistic missile submarine is a submarine capable of deploying submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs) with nuclear warheads. These submarines became a major weapon system in the Cold War because of their nuclear deterrence capability. They can fire missiles thousands of kilometres (miles) from their targets, and acoustic quieting makes them difficult to detect (see acoustic signature), thus making them a survivable deterrent in the event of a first strike and a key element of the mutual assured destruction policy of nuclear deterrence. Many ballistic missile submarine policies also include provisions for nuclear first strike as well. For these reasons, 70% of nuclear warheads in the United States are carried by ballistic missile submarines.
The deployment of ballistic missile submarines is dominated by the United States,  Russia (following the collapse of the Soviet Union) and China. Smaller numbers are in service with France, the United Kingdom and India.
North Korea is also suspected to have an experimental submarine that is diesel-electric powered. Israel also has diesel-electric submarines carrying nuclear weapons, however their nuclear warheads are mounted onto cruise missiles, not onto ballistic missiles.
Ballistic missile submarines should be distinguished from so-called nuclear submarines, which does not refer to a submarine carrying nuclear weapons, but instead refers to submarines with a nuclear propulsion engine.
